rv.q: It’s messy, fascinating, and heedless of the rules —and isn’t it nice that an Academy Award-winning Yale professor of playwrighting can still write something like that?
Ms. Blakk for President certainly has my vote, but I wish I could cast it with more enthusiasm.
The “purposes of the play” seem less a profile of a person or a historic accounting than a lively entertainment, albeit one punctuated with a polemic.
But Ms. Blakk for President is sprawling at the expense of creating a truly rich and focused study of character, time, place, and politics.
The marvelous Ms. Blakk for President is based on Smith’s story.
That said, for the engaged audience member, it’s absolutely dazzling.
While fun and entertaining, doesn't reach deep enough to uproot or unsettle.
Ms. Blakk for President takes an extraordinary episode of American political history and turns it, not into compelling drama, but into 105 minutes of well-done, good-hearted fun.
Ms. Blakk for President can’t quite find Terence’s personal stakes inside the bigger movement, even with the death of Mark’s partner from AIDS-related complications.
Yet Ms. Blakk for President remains a musical in search of its own identity.
As a time-warp drag show with plenty of surface glitz, Ms. Blakk for President can be a lot of fun.
Even Sawyer Smith's phenomenal performance as both dancer and vocalist can't quite overcome the residual pall.

cn.t: Critics find this vibrant account of drag queen Joan Jett Blakk's 1992 presidential campaign visually striking and energetically staged, but most feel it prioritizes spectacle and celebration over deeper examination of its activist subject matter.

vr.q: Ms. Blakk for President is a rapturous retelling of a remarkable story, carrying the passion, joy, and resistance that made the story possible.
I think it's successful as a history lesson, but not so much as a dramatic piece of theater.
